nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: 1994.  DMS | R. Grant Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution, Florida.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Goldspotted Killifish
Scientific Name: Floridichthys carpio

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Atheriniformes
	Family: Cyprinodontidae

Other Common Names: Goldspotted Topminnow

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Gunther 1866).
	Reference for Classification (1914)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sold as an aquarium fish (2368).

Recreational:  Captured and utilized as an aquarium fish (2368).

Ecological Role:  The abundance of Floridichthys makes it a valuable food source for piscine and avian predators in shallow water habitats.

Indicator:  Seagrass beds present, good water quality with high dissolved oxygen levels.

nodes.title: Overall
nodes.body: A subtropical/tropical species found from S.E. Florida and Gulf of Mexico and Belize (788: Gilmore pers. obs.).  In Florida, two populations, west coast population from Cape San Blas to Florida Keys and Miami.  East coast population from Ft. Pierce to Volusia County. (2382).

nodes.title: Within Study Area
nodes.body: Common from the northern portion of the Indian River Lagoon to Fort Pierce area (2344; 2320; 848; 993; 2386; 2215).  Also captured from Boca Raton south (2383; 2382 ).  This species is not abundant in the southern half of the Indian River Lagoon (887; 2362, 993).  Due to the lack of morphological and electrophoretic variation in the Florida populations Duggins et al. (1983) question the small distributional gap.

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Epibenthic/benthic omnivore of vegetated saline estuaries of the Florida and Yucatan peninsulas (2382; 788).

Migrations and Movements:  Moves back and forth with the tide to maintain position in shallow water habitat (2384).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Protected beaches and estuarine shorelines, Thalassia and Halodule seagrass beds with clear shallow water with sand, marl and calcareous substrate (2382; 788; 2381; 2384; 2156). Orientates in the water column in relation to depth and tidal movement, with offshore habitat limited by presence of large predators and inshore by depth and water quality.
Juvenile: Juveniles require the shallower depths were the adults require deeper depths (less than 1.5m) for mating and feeding (2384).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Sand, marl, calcareous substrate and seagrass beds (2382; 788; 2381; 2384; 2156).

Physical/Chemical:  Temperature tolerance have been recorded as high as 37.7 C  (100 F) in isolated pools and as low as 14 C (2384; 378).  Kaill showed that dissolved oxygen is an important limiting factor for Floridichthys survival. Floridichthys shows stress at dissolved oxygen levels of 6-8 ppm and signs of incapacitation at levels of 4-5 ppm.  Salinity tolerances range from 14 ppt to 87 ppt  with optimum greater than 25 ppt (2381; 2385; 2384).  Nordlie and Walsh suggest that Floridichthys can move into freshwater but only on a short term basis.

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Mode: Gonochoristic, oviparous, polygamous, iteroparous.

Mating and Spawning:  Spawning appears to take place year round with a peak occurring in late summer.  Gravid females with mature eggs were collected in November through February as well as other months (2384).  Males establish territories in when water depth and water quality are favorable.  Sand bottom tide pools are a frequent spawning site.  Females may spawn with several different males, dependent upon male population density (2384).  Courtship usually involves complex displays and courtship maneuvers (2384).
Fecundity:  No information

Growth and Development
Egg: The demersal eggs of Floridichthys are about 1.4 mm in diameter when water hardened.  One or two of the chorionic threads which extend from the surface of the eggs are very long.  They function as an entangling device, for the retention of the eggs in algae or sand spawning substrate.  The egg includes one oil droplet.  Hatching occurs in from 9 to 12 days.  In an aquarium with 26.0 C (80 F)  water temperature, 10 days were required (2384).
Larvae:  The prolarvae have a well developed pattern of pigmentation, which is essentially that of the epidermal layer of the adult.  Until their air bladders are filled, they lie on the bottom with caudal fin curved for long periods of time.  They attack food items with a sudden lunge, and then drift to the bottom to remain motionless.  After filling their air bladders, they assume adult habits, but live in very shallow water (2384).
Juvenile:  As juveniles, they join the schooling population but in shallower depths than the adults (2384)

Adult:  Gunter (1945) and Kilby (1955) conclude that Floridichthys is essentially restricted to a one year life span, with the smaller winter populations recruited from late summer the young  (2384).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Gut contents from Card Sound research consisted of  plant material, polychaetes, copepods, amphipods, unidentified crustaceans, mollusks (marginellids) (2381).  The succession of algae from spring well into the summer allows increasing amounts of food and cover for the Floridichthys population (2384). Opportunism describes the feeding habits of virtually all cyprinodonts.  Common foods of Floridichthys are plants obtained by extensive grazing.  Much of this is in the form of epiphytes scraped from the surface of the higher plants by tricuspid teeth.  Stomach contents reveal a high proportion of unicellular algae such as the filamentous and encrusting diatoms, and large quantities of indigestible material such as sand.  However, they readily attack carrion and small crustaceans (2384).  Grazing takes place upon Sargassum, particularly if fresh and with the resident organisms still intact (2384).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The abundance of Floridichthys makes it a valuable food source for piscine and avian predators in shallow water habitats.
